newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean union workers revive strike threat.
newsitem.headline: South Korean union workers revive strike threat.

text.p: South Korean union workers on Monday revived threats for an all-out strike this week if their demands went ignored in President Kim Young-sam's address on Tuesday.
"We want to hear President Kim say he would accept our demands," said Yoon Young-mo, a leader of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions.
"If he does not, we will launch an all-out strike very soon," he added.

President Kim is expected to speak to the nation in a televised address Tuesday morning on various national issues, including the loan scandal which followed the financial collapse of Hanbo Steel, a government spokesman said.
Unions have demanded the repeal of a controversial new labour law that makes it easier for employers to lay off workers and replace strikers.
Union leaders said they would also look for more positive results from parliamentary debates which reopened last week.
The confederation also said proposals from opposition parties were not "satisfactory" as they failed to recognise the teachers' union.
"Their proposals fell short of our expectations as they left out teachers' right to join unions," Yoon said.
About 1,000 members of the outlawed teachers' union rallied in central Seoul on Monday and marched to the ruling party's building, demanding legal recognition of their union.

The two main opposition parties -- the National Congress for New Politics and the United Liberal Democratic Party -- submitted a joint proposal to a labour committee in parliament, calling for the abandonment of a clause which allows worker layoffs.
The confederation's earlier plan to go on strikes on February 18 was postponed to between February 24-28 as they wanted to see how parliament would handle the revision of the new labour law.
The National Assembly reopened on February 17 for a 30-day session to discuss possible revision of the labour law and probe into the Hanbo scandal.

The collapse of South Korea's Hanbo Steel Co after it borrowed five trillion won ($5.8 billion), about 20 times its net worth, has exposed the need to eliminate corruption by speeding up financial restructuring, analysts said on Monday.
Opposition parties called the loans the biggest financial scandal in the nation's history and have accused the government of peddling influence to pressure banks into offering loans.
Almost a month of strikes erupted from late December last year, after the ruling New Korea party passed the law in parliament while opposition members were sleeping.
